columns.name: statement

columns.help: '<cause> increases | decreases | has no effect on | has mixed effects on <effect>' — no numbers, no 'significantly', no method, setting or population; for not_causal the sentence's finding in one line

columns.label: Cause
columns.help: the cause as the abstract names it: a short noun phrase, no transformation ('earnings', not 'log earnings'); null for not_causal

columns.name: effect
columns.label: Effect
columns.help: the effect as the abstract names it; null for not_causal

columns.name: cause_construct
columns.label: Cause construct
columns.help: the broader construct the cause is an indicator of, when this paper measures one construct through several variables: 'tax incentives' for 'marginal net-of-tax rate'. Write it the SAME way in every claim that indicates it; null when the cause IS the construct

columns.name: effect_construct
columns.label: Effect construct
columns.help: the broader construct the effect is an indicator of: 'mental health' for 'use of psychological assistance', 'prescriptions for mental-health conditions' and 'opioid prescriptions' — three claims, one construct, written identically in all three. Null when the effect IS the construct

columns.name: construct_basis
columns.label: Construct basis
columns.help: stated = the paper itself presents these variables as measuring the construct ('we study mental health, measured by …'); inferred = treating them as indicators of one construct is YOUR reading. Null when no construct is named

columns.name: construct_note
columns.label: Construct assumption
columns.help: the auxiliary assumption in one sentence — 'opioid prescriptions are treated as an indicator of mental health'. It is what a reviewer judges; write it whenever the basis is inferred

columns.name: sign
columns.label: Sign
columns.help: in the paper's own orientation: + increases, - decreases, 0 the authors report testing and finding no effect, mixed the sign differs across groups or settings and the text says so; null for not_causal

columns.name: estimand
columns.label: Estimand
columns.help: a short key for WHAT is estimated, identical for every estimate of the same quantity and different whenever the quantity differs: '<claim>/<subgroup>/<horizon>' ('S1/men/years-0-1', 'S3/all/5y', 'S2/all/discrete-exposure'). Exactly ONE estimate per estimand is the preferred one (role main); the others are the same quantity measured again

columns.name: role
columns.label: Role
columns.help: main = the estimate the authors would point to for this finding; supporting = another specification of the same finding they rely on; robustness; heterogeneity = a subgroup split of it

columns.name: exhibit
columns.label: Exhibit
columns.help: which exhibit shows the ANALYSIS this estimate comes from — a table, a figure, or none when the paper reports the analysis only in prose ('in unreported regressions …'). Fill it even when the number itself is not printed there: the exhibit is what tells a reader the estimator, the sample and the specification

columns.name: source_table
columns.label: Table / figure
columns.help: the exhibit as printed: 'Table 3', 'Table A2', 'Figure 4' — the analysis this estimate belongs to, even when its value is only stated in the text; null only when the paper shows no exhibit for it

columns.name: panel
columns.label: Panel
columns.help: the panel label ('A', 'B') or null when the table has no panels

columns.name: column
columns.label: Column
columns.help: the column label exactly as printed: '(2)', 'Percent'; null for a figure

columns.name: row_label
columns.label: Row
columns.help: the row label of the coefficient as printed; for a figure the annotation or series it comes from

columns.name: subgroup
columns.label: Subgroup
columns.help: who this estimate is for when the column or panel restricts the claim's population: 'men', 'women', 'top earnings quartile', 'manufacturing'. Null when it covers the claim's whole population. The claim itself stays general — the subgroup lives here, so the estimates for men and women stay apart
samples: All immigrants; employment with wage subsidy
Social assistance recipients; employment with wage subsidy

columns.name: horizon
columns.label: Horizon
columns.help: the window this estimate covers when the paper reports several: 'years 0-1', 'year 5', 'the post-reform period', 'long run'. Null when the paper reports only one. As printed in the panel or column heading
samples: total effect on restricted mean duration over 4 years

columns.name: horizon_lo
columns.label: Horizon from (years)
columns.help: the window's inclusive LOWER edge in years since the event: 'year 4' → 4, 'years 6-10' → 6, 'within five years' → 0. Null when the paper gives no event clock (calendar months, cross-section years) — then `horizon` alone carries the label

columns.name: horizon_hi
columns.label: Horizon to (years)
columns.help: the window's inclusive UPPER edge in years since the event: 'year 4' → 4, 'years 6-10' → 10, 'within five years' → 5. A point-in-time estimate has horizon_lo = horizon_hi. Null when there is no event clock

columns.name: horizon_kind
columns.label: Horizon kind
columns.help: what the estimate IS over that window — the interval alone does not disambiguate: `point` (the effect AT year 4), `average` (the mean effect over years 0-5), `cumulative` (the total accumulated within five years), `difference` (a change between two dates). Null when horizon_lo/hi are null

columns.name: outcome_variable
columns.label: Outcome
columns.help: the dependent variable of that column as the paper names it

columns.name: regressor
columns.label: Regressor
columns.help: the coefficient's regressor as printed (the treatment, the instrumented variable, the policy variable)

columns.name: value_from
columns.label: Number from
columns.help: where the NUMBER comes from: printed = it is printed in the exhibit (a table cell, a figure annotation); text = the exhibit does not print it but the paper states it in prose ('women visit psychologists 0.10 more times per year'); absent = the paper reports no number for this estimate. Only a printed table value can be cross-checked against the transcribed cells

columns.name: point_estimate
columns.label: Point estimate
columns.help: the coefficient exactly as printed in that cell (sign, every digit; stars, parentheses and commas stripped); for a figure only a value the figure PRINTS (an annotation) — never read off an axis; null when no number is printed

columns.name: estimate_se
columns.label: Standard error
columns.help: the standard error printed for that coefficient (the parenthesised value); null when the table prints a t-statistic or p-value instead, or nothing

columns.name: treatment_relation
columns.label: Treatment relation
columns.help: direct = the regressor measures the cause itself; proxy; assignment = a treatment-group, reform or instrument indicator standing in for the cause

columns.name: outcome_relation
columns.label: Outcome relation
columns.help: direct = the outcome measures the effect itself; proxy

columns.name: sign_consistent
columns.label: Sign consistent
columns.help: read in its OWN variable orientation, does the estimate agree with the claim's direction? (a net-of-tax-rate elasticity of +0.2 agrees with 'the tax rate decreases income'); null when there is no estimate or it cannot be told. A disagreeing result is still a match — that is a finding

columns.label: Why
columns.help: one sentence: why this result operationalises the claim (and, for a comparison, which side it is)

a subgroup of high-income savers, individuals in the upper half of the income distribution
quasi-experimental difference-in-differences design using the introduced tax deduction threshold as the cutoff

The anchor names the outcome ('all types of savings') and the result ('full crowding-out') but not the cause; the introduction states that the paper documents full crowding-out in retirement savings for the 2010 tax reform and that the outcomes of interest are whether the reform increased other types of savings.

Six separate dependent variables, one regression per printed row: annual life-long pension contributions, capital pension contributions, mortgage debt repayments, bank debt repayments (net of bank deposits changes), bank deposits, and financial assets. All are measured as annual year-on-year changes in stock/flow variables in DKK.

Baseline 2SLS: 57 cents of every DKK 1 reduction in annuity contributions goes into life-long pension schemes, the largest alternative-savings response in the sum that gives full crowding-out. The gift of time? School starting age and mental health
Age at kindergarten entry decreases total difficulties
Using linked Danish survey and register data, we estimate the causal effect of age at kindergarten entry on mental health.
Our results indicate that a 1-year increase in the school starting age leads to significantly improved mental health (i.e., reducing the “total difficulties” scores at age 7 by 0.6 SD).
Danish children in the Danish National Birth Cohort
fuzzy regression-discontinuity design on exact date of birth around the January 1 school starting age cutoff
reducing the “total difficulties” scores at age 7 by 0.6 SD

The abstract sentence only announces that the causal effect of age at kindergarten entry on mental health is estimated; the introduction supplies the direction and the concrete outcome (total difficulties score).
Standardized SDQ measures at age 7 (one per row): total difficulties, emotional symptoms, conduct problems, inattention/hyperactivity, peer problems, pro-social behavior

The controls specification of the reduced-form RD on standardized age-7 total difficulties, scaled by the first stage, is the estimate that produces the stated 0.6 SD improvement; the body states the preferred estimates are those conditional on controls. Derivation: Reduced-form ITT on total difficulties at age 7 = -0.12 (Table 4, col. 2, row 'Total difficulties') divided by the first stage 0.20 (Table 2, col. 2, day_i > 0) = -0.60 SD, the 0.6 SD stated in the introduction.

Spillover effects of stricter immigration policies
The paper provides evidence that national immigration policies produce spillover effects on migration behavior, estimated from stricter family reunification rules in Denmark.
We provide evidence for the existence of spillover effects of national immigration policies by estimating the effect of stricter family reunification rules in Denmark on migration behavior.
The question we ask in this paper is whether those unable to reunify in one country, due to stricter immigration policies, nonetheless are able to bring their partners to Europe by migrating to…
Denmark, with migration to neighboring European countries
individuals affected by stricter family reunification rules

We find that for any given parity, the human capital profile of children in smaller families dominates that of large families, and that the average child's education decreases as family size…
We also find that family size has a strong negative effect on the average education in the household.

Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and C (2020)
Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?
parental leave take-up has no effect on total labor inputs
We find little evidence that parental leave take-up has negative effects on firms and coworkers overall.
On the basis of an approximate measure of firm's total hours, we see no indications that firm's total labor inputs are affected by parental leave
small firms (fewer than 30 employees) in Denmark
small firms employing a woman who gives birth and takes parental leave
dynamic difference-in-differences comparing firms of women who become pregnant with firms of comparable women who do not
the 95% confidence interval from our preferred specification excludes effect sizes such that having 1% of the workforce on leave reduces total hours by more than 0.19%
Abstract announces only 'little evidence of negative effects on firms'; the introduction names the outcome (total labor inputs) and states the null.
Hours at firm (% relative to baseline)

Five separate firm-level outcomes, one regression per printed coefficient row, each measured in the event year (t = 0) and differenced from the baseline year (t = -2): (i) parental leave days at firm; (ii) number of employees at firm (% relative to baseline); (iii) new hires at firm; (iv) turnover at firm; (v) hours at firm (% relative to baseline).
Hours at firm (% relative to baseline)

Firm total hours relative to baseline, the paper's measure of total labor inputs, scaled per 1% of the workforce on leave; the body calls the percent-of-workforce specification preferred for outcomes measured relative to baseline. Derivation: Lower 95% CI bound from the preferred column 3 estimate: −0.0479 − 1.96 × 0.0713 = −0.188 ≈ −0.19% when 1% of the workforce goes on leave.

Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?
parental leave take-up increases total wage bill
total wage bill (including wages paid to workers on leave)
We find little evidence that parental leave take-up has negative effects on firms and coworkers overall.
Together with the temporary increase in hires and retention, these changes lead to an increase in the treatment firms' total wage bill.
small firms (fewer than 30 employees) in Denmark
small firms employing a woman who gives birth and takes parental leave
dynamic difference-in-differences comparing firms of women who become pregnant with firms of comparable women who do not
Abstract announces effects on firms in general terms; the introduction names the wage bill and gives the direction.
Firm's wage bill (% relative to baseline)

Three separate firm-level outcomes, one regression per printed coefficient row, each measured in the event year (t = 0) and differenced from the baseline year (t = -2): (i) firm's wage bill (% relative to baseline); (ii) firm's wage bill excluding paid leave (% relative to baseline); (iii) firm's total variable cost (% relative to baseline).
Firm's wage bill (% relative to baseline)
Firm wage bill including paid leave relative to baseline, per 1% of the workforce on leave; the body names column 3 the preferred 2SLS estimate (+0.27%).

The Temporality of Being NEET: A Longitu (2020)
The Temporality of Being NEET: A Longitudinal Study of NEET Occurrences among Young Adults in Denmark
Being NEET has no effect on risk of social exclusion
The article demonstrates how four out of five young adults labelled NEET cannot be characterized as being at risk of social exclusion.
The study exploits high quality, longitudinal data from Danish administrative registers and demonstrates that being NEET does not express a risk of social exclusion as such.
young adults labelled NEET, aged 16 to 24
sequence analysis and clustering of longitudinal Danish administrative register data (descriptive, no causal identification)
four out of five young adults labelled NEET cannot be characterized as being at risk of social exclusion

The abstract anchor states the share of NEET-labelled young adults who cannot be characterized as at risk; the introduction supplies the explicit direction ('being NEET does not express a risk of social exclusion as such').
cluster A (few, short NEET occurrences; 71.1% of study population)

Largest cluster (71.1%): only ~12% are NEET at the end of the nine-year window, so for the bulk of the labelled-NEET population the status is brief and seasonal rather than a trajectory of exclusion — the estimate carrying the 'four out of five' claim. Derivation: Cluster A n = 11,593 (71.1% of 16,314) + cluster B n = 1,327 (8.1%) = 12,920/16,314 = 79.2%, i.e. 'four out of five'; cluster A's combined NEET share stays at 0.07-0.12 across the window.

peer ability increases later labor market outcomes
Our findings suggest that peer ability is an important determinant of students' drop out decisions as well as later labor market outcomes.
First, we estimate the effects of peer quality on later labor market outcomes.
the entire population of students entering higher education
idiosyncratic variation in peer composition across cohorts within the same education and institution

Childhood disadvantage decreases the returns to genetic endowments for educational attainment.
returns to genetic endowments for educational attainment
We show that the returns to genetic endowments, measured by a polygenic score for educational attainment, are significantly attenuated by childhood disadvantage.
We show that the genetic influences on educational attainment and academic achievement are 20-40% smaller in the group that experienced disadvantage.

mortgage interest deduction has no effect on homeownership

Home Prices, Fertility, and Early-Life Health Outcomes
Home prices increase the likelihood of giving birth.
Using rich population register data among women aged 20-44 who own a home, we find that for each 100,000 DKK increase in home prices (equivalent to $12,000), the likelihood of giving birth increases…
Our findings suggest that there is a positive effect of home price increases on fertility: a 100,000 DK (approximately $12,000 in 2006, adjusting for purchasing power parity) increase in home prices…
women aged 20-44 who own a home

one-year change in home value related to the likelihood of giving birth in the subsequent year, among women who became homeowners during 1993-2004, following Lovenheim and Mumford (2013); population register data
for each 100,000 DKK increase in home prices (equivalent to $12,000), the likelihood of giving birth increases by 0.27 percentage points or 2.32%
